{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output_head": "# Chat Bots Design Notes

## Data Model (`User` + `User::Bot`)

Bots are represented in the `users` table with `role: :bot` (`enum :role, %i[ member administrator bot ]`):

- **`creator_id`**: Foreign key to `users` (`belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", optional: true`), recording which chat member created the bot. Because `User::Role#can_administer?` checks `administrator? || self == record&.creator`, creators and administrators automatically have permission to manage a bot while other regular members do not.
- **`bot_token` & `bot_key`**: Active bots receive a unique 24-character `SecureRandom.base58` `bot_token` on creation. The externally visible bot code (`User#bot_key`) is `"#{id}-#{bot_token}"`. `User.authenticate_bot(bot_key)` looks up the active bot by primary key `id` and compares `bot_token` in constant time via `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare`.
- **Deactivation (Deletion)**: Deleting a bot calls `User#deactivate`, which sets `status: :deactivated`, clears `bot_token: nil`, and removes non-direct room memberships while preserving historical messages authored by the bot.
- **Room Memberships**: Because bots are `User` records with `status: :active`, they automatically join all open rooms via `after_create_commit :grant_membership_to_open_rooms` (and `Rooms::Open#grant_access_to_all_users`) and appear alongside human users in closed/direct room member selectors (`User.active`). Human-only flows (`/account/edit` member list, `/session`, session transfers, IP bans) scope queries with `User.without_bots`.

## Bot HTTP API (`Messages::ByBotsController`)

- **Endpoint**: `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` (`constraints: { room_id: /[^\/]+/, bot_key: /[^\/]+/ }`).
- **Raw Body Handling**: `curl -d "..."` sends `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` by default even though the payload is raw text (which may contain `%`, `+`, `&`, etc.). `Messages::ByBotsController` sets `wrap_parameters false` and `request.request_parameters = {}` in `process_action` before Rails instrumentation accesses `request.filtered_parameters`, preventing Rack/Rails form/JSON parameter parsers from raising `400 Bad Request` on raw bodies. The raw UTF-8 body is read from `request.raw_post`.
- **Validation & Extension Point for Attachments**: `Message` validates `ensure_body_or_attachment_present` (`body.blank? && body.body&.attachables.blank? && !attachment?`). If future features add file attachment uploads for bots (e.g., binary bodies by `Content-Type` or `multipart/form-data`), `Messages::ByBotsController#create` can attach the file and call `@message.process_attachment` before `@message.broadcast_create`.
- **Broadcasts & Push Notifications**: Setting `Current.user = bot` sets `message.creator = bot`. Saving triggers `Room#receive` (`unread_memberships` + `Room::PushMessageJob`), and `@message.broadcast_create` appends the message via Turbo Streams and notifies `UnreadRoomsChannel`.
---
## Development

### Setting up

First, get everything installed and configured with:

```sh
bin/setup
```

This installs the system packages Campfire needs (SQLite, ffmpeg), the right Ruby version (via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev)), and the app's gems; prepares the database; and starts Redis (in a Docker container called `campfire-redis`, if it isn't already running locally).

If you want to start over at any point, run:

```sh
bin/setup --reset
```

### Running the server

Start the development server with:

```sh
bin/dev
```

You'll be able to access the app at http://localhost:3000.

On first run you'll be guided through creating your admin account, and you can sign in with that account from then on.

Note that Campfire needs Redis (for Action Cable, caching, and background jobs), so if you've restarted your machine or stopped the container, `docker start campfire-redis` will bring it back.

### Web Push notifications

Campfire uses VAPID (Voluntary Application Server Identification) keys to send browser push notifications. For notifications to work in development you'll need to generate a key pair and set these environment variables:

- `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`

You can generate a fresh pair (along with a secret key base, which you can ignore in development) by running:

```sh
script/admin/generate-secrets
```

### Running tests

Run the unit tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test
```

And the browser-based system tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test:system
```

Before pushing your changes, you can run the full CI suite locally - style checks, security audits, and all the tests - with a single command:

```sh
bin/ci
```

### Contributing

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
If you'd like to contribute your changes back, please read our [contributing guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md) first.

      if user = active.bot.find_by(id: bot_id)

require "surfguard"

module RestrictedHTTP
  class Violation < StandardError; end

  # The address policy lives in the surfguard gem so this app, Basecamp, HEY and
  # Fizzy classify "internal" the same way instead of each keeping a copy that
  # drifts. The callers here hand a bare hostname in and pin the address that
  # comes back, so this stays a hostname-in, address-out shim.
  module PrivateNetworkGuard
    extend self

    # A hostname that resolves to nothing (NXDOMAIN, timeout, empty answer)
    # raises Surfguard::Unresolvable, which we let propagate as a lookup failure
    # -- the same way the old Resolv.getaddress guard raised Resolv::ResolvError,
    # and the callers here already treat it as a fetch failure. The Violation is
    # reserved for a host that resolves to a blocked address (an empty list back
    # from resolve_public_ips), so a transient DNS miss is never misreported as
    # an SSRF attempt.
    def resolve(hostname)
      Surfguard.resolve_public_ips(hostname).first or
        raise Violation.new("Attempt to access private IP via #{hostname}")
    end

    def private_ip?(ip)
      Surfguard.blocked_address?(ip)
    end
  end
end

class Opengraph::Fetch
  ALLOWED_DOCUMENT_CONTENT_TYPE = "text/html"
  MAX_BODY_SIZE = 5.megabytes
  MAX_REDIRECTS = 10

  class TooManyRedirectsError < StandardError; end
  class RedirectDeniedError < StandardError; end

  def fetch_document(url, ip: RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard.resolve(url.host))
    request(url, Net::HTTP::Get, ip: ip) do |response|
      return body_if_acceptable(response)
    end
  end

  def fetch_content_type(url, ip: RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard.resolve(url.host))
    request(url, Net::HTTP::Head, ip: ip) do |response|
      return response["Content-Type"]
    end
  end

  private
    def request(url, request_class, ip:)
      MAX_REDIRECTS.times do
        Net::HTTP.start(url.host, url.port, ipaddr: ip, use_ssl: url.scheme == "https") do |http|
          http.request request_class.new(url) do |response|
            if response.is_a?(Net::HTTPRedirection)
              url, ip = resolve_redirect(response["location"])
            else
              yield response
            end
          end
        end
      end

      raise TooManyRedirectsError
    end

    def resolve_redirect(location)
      url = URI.parse(location)
      raise RedirectDeniedError unless url.is_a?(URI::HTTP)
      [ url, RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard.resolve(url.host) ]
    end

    def body_if_acceptable(response)
      size_restricted_body(response) if response_valid?(response)
    end

    def size_restricted_body(response)
      # We've already checked the Content-Length header, to try to avoid reading
      # the body of any large responses. But that header could be wrong or
      # missing. To be on the safe side, we'll read the body in chunks, and bail
      # if it runs over our size limit.
      StringIO.new.tap do |body|
        response.read_body do |chunk|
          return nil if body.string.bytesize + chunk.bytesize > MAX_BODY_SIZE
          body << chunk
        end
      end.string
    end

    def response_valid?(response)
      status_valid?(response) && content_type_valid?(response) && content_length_valid?(response)
    end

    def status_valid?(response)
      response.is_a?(Net::HTTPOK)
    end

    def content_type_valid?(response)
      response.content_type == ALLOWED_DOCUMENT_CONTENT_TYPE
    end

    def content_length_valid?(response)
      response.content_length.to_i <= MAX_BODY_SIZE
    end

class User::BotTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  setup do
    Current.user = users(:kevin)
  end

  teardown do
    Current.reset
  end

  test "create_bot! creates an active bot owned by Current.user with a unique bot_key" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot")

    assert bot.bot?
    assert bot.active?
    assert_equal users(:kevin), bot.creator
    assert bot.bot_token.present?
    assert_equal "#{bot.id}-#{bot.bot_token}", bot.bot_key
    assert_includes users(:kevin).bots, bot
  end

  test "human users do not get a bot_token or bot_key" do
    user = User.create!(name: "Human", email_address: "human@example.com", password: "secret123456")

    assert user.member?
    assert_nil user.bot_token
    assert_nil user.bot_key
    assert_includes User.without_bots, user
  end

  test "bot requires a name" do
    bot = User.new_bot(name: "")
    assert_not bot.valid?
    assert_includes bot.errors[:name], "can't be blank"
  end

  test "new bot automatically joins all open rooms" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot")

    assert_equal Rooms::Open.pluck(:id).sort, bot.rooms.pluck(:id).sort
    assert_not_includes bot.rooms, rooms(:designers)
  end

  test "new open room grants access to existing active bots but not deactivated bots" do
    active_bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Active Bot")
    deleted_bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deleted Bot")
    deleted_bot.deactivate

    open_room = Rooms::Open.create!(name: "Announcements", creator: users(:david))

    assert_includes open_room.users, active_bot
    assert_not_includes open_room.users, deleted_bot
  end

  test "authenticate_bot verifies bot_key securely" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot")

    assert_equal bot, User.authenticate_bot(bot.bot_key)
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("#{bot.id}-wrongtoken")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("999999-#{bot.bot_token}")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("#{users(:david).id}-#{bot.bot_token}")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("malformed_without_dash")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot(nil)
  end

  test "deactivating a bot revokes its bot_key and removes non-direct memberships" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot")
    old_key = bot.bot_key

    bot.deactivate

    assert bot.reload.deactivated?
    assert_nil bot.bot_token
    assert_nil bot.bot_key
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot(old_key)
    assert_empty bot.memberships.without_direct_rooms
  end

    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Kevin Bot")

    assert users(:kevin).can_administer?(bot)
    assert users(:david).can_administer?(bot)
    assert_not users(:jz).can_administer?(bot)
    assert_not bot.can_administer?(bot)
  end
end

      assert_select ".message__body", text: /Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅/
    end
  end

  test "triggers web push notifications exactly as a human-authored message would" do
    expected_deliveries = Push::Subscription.count
    assert expected_deliveries > 0

    perform_enqueued_jobs only: Room::PushMessageJob do
      WebPush.expects(:payload_send).times(expected_deliveries).with do |kwargs|
        payload = JSON.parse(kwargs[:message])
        payload["title"] == @room.name &&
          payload.dig("options", "body") == "Deploy Bot: Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅"
      end

      post_bot_message @room.id, @bot.bot_key, "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅"
    end

    wait_for_web_push_delivery_pool_tasks(expected_deliveries)
  end

  test "returns 422 Unprocessable Content for empty or whitespace-only body without attachment" do
    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post_bot_message @room.id, @bot.bot_key, ""
      assert_response :unprocessable_content

      post_bot_message @room.id, @bot.bot_key, "   \n\t  ", content_type: "text/plain"
      assert_response :unprocessable_content
    end
  end

  test "returns 404 Not Found for nonexistent room id or closed room bot is not a member of" do
    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post_bot_message 99999999, @bot.bot_key, "Hello"
      assert_response :not_found

      post_bot_message "bad-room", @bot.bot_key, "Hello"
      assert_response :not_found

      # Closed room that @bot has not joined
      assert_not_includes @bot.rooms, rooms(:designers)
      post_bot_message rooms(:designers).id, @bot.bot_key, "Hello"
      assert_response :not_found
    end

    # Once added to the closed room, bot can post
    rooms(:designers).memberships.grant_to(@bot)
    post_bot_message rooms(:designers).id, @bot.bot_key, "Hello Designers"
    assert_response :created
  end

  test "returns 401 Unauthorized for invalid bot code" do
    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post_bot_message @room.id, "invalid-bot-code", "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized

      post_bot_message @room.id, "#{@bot.id}-wrongtoken", "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized

      post_bot_message @room.id, "bad.code.with.dots", "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized

      # Invalid bot code with bad room id still returns 401 Unauthorized without leaking room existence
      post_bot_message 99999999, "invalid-bot-code", "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized
    end
  end

  test "deleted bot can no longer post messages while keeping previous messages" do
    post_bot_message @room.id, @bot.bot_key, "Before deletion"
    assert_response :created
    previous_message = Message.last

    old_key = @bot.bot_key
    @bot.deactivate

    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post_bot_message @room.id, old_key, "After deletion"
      assert_response :unauthorized
    end

    assert previous_message.reload.persisted?
    assert_equal "Deploy Bot", previous_message.creator.name
  end

  private
    def post_bot_message(room_id, bot_key, body, content_type: "application/x-www-form-urlencoded")
      post "/rooms/#{room_id}/#{bot_key}/messages",
        params: +body,
        headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => content_type }
    end

    def wait_for_web_push_delivery_pool_tasks(count)
      pool = Rails.configuration.x.web_push_pool.delivery_pool
      start = Time.now
      while pool.completed_task_count < count
        raise "Timeout waiting for web push pool tasks" if Time.now - start > 1.0
        sleep 0.02
      end
    end

class SendingMessagesTest < ApplicationSystemTestCase
  setup do
    sign_in "jz@37signals.com"
    join_room rooms(:designers)
  end

  test "sending messages between two users" do
    using_session("Kevin") do
      sign_in "kevin@37signals.com"
      join_room rooms(:designers)
    end

  end

    using_session("Kevin") do
      sign_in "kevin@37signals.com"
      join_room rooms(:designers)

    end

      join_room rooms(:designers)

    end

It says, "Saving the form with an empty webhook URL removes the bot's webhook." That suggests we need to think about how this interacts with our existing models.

I'm considering two main options based on the Campfire model:

**Option A:** A `Webhook` model (`webhooks` table with `user_id` and `url`, `has_one :webhook, dependent: :destroy` on `User::Bot`). We could have a `webhook_url` getter/setter on `User::Bot` so that it integrates seamlessly with Rails form helpers (`form.text_field :webhook_url` or `form.url_field :webhook_url`) on `@bot`, where `@bot.webhook` is the `Webhook` record that is created/updated on presence and deleted on empty `webhook_url` OR the bot is deactivated. The key here is that `User.create_bot!(name: "...", webhook_url: "...")` also works!

**Option B:** Consider the `Webhook` as a separate model (`Webhook < ApplicationRecord` with `belongs_to :user`). AND `User::Bot` defines `has_one :webhook, dependent: :destroy`, `webhook_url`, `webhook_url=`?
OR could `webhook_url` be a column on `users` instead of a dedicated `Webhook` model?

The `Webhook` model encapsulating the delivery logic is appealing: `webhook.deliver(message)` or `Webhook::DeliveryJob` (or a `Bot::WebhookDeliveryJob`). The prompt's phrasing clearly implies that: "A bot may have an optional webhook URL" and "Saving the form with an empty webhook URL removes the bot's webhook." Considering future enhancements like event subscriptions, delivery logs, etc., the `Webhook` model seems more scalable.

With this structure, we get both: `@bot.webhook` (a `Webhook` model record, destroyed appropriately) and `@bot.webhook_url` / `@bot.webhook_url=` for easy integration with form helpers and direct updates.

However, edge cases during validation errors are crucial! Say we have an existing bot with a `webhook` record and the user tries to update the bot. What happens if validation fails (e.g., empty `name` and `webhook_url`)? We need to ensure that the form displays the original `webhook_url` and that the `webhook` record isn't prematurely destroyed. #!/usr/bin/env ruby

require "json"
require "yaml"

class ProcessMonitor
  SIGNALS = %w[ INT TERM CLD ]

  def initialize(procfile)
    @procs = process_list(procfile)
    handle_signals

    @procs.each &:start
    @procs.each &:wait
  end

  private
    def process_list(procfile)
      config = YAML.load_file(procfile)
      config.map { |name, cmd| MonitoredProcess.new(name, cmd) }
    end

    def handle_signals
      SIGNALS.each do |signal|
        Signal.trap(signal) do
          @procs.each &:terminate
        end
      end
    end
end

class MonitoredProcess
  def initialize(name, cmd)
    @name, @cmd = name, cmd
  end

  def start
    @pid = Process.spawn(@cmd)
  end

  def wait
    Process.wait @pid
  rescue Errno::ECHILD
    nil
  end

  def terminate
    Process.kill "TERM", @pid
  rescue Errno::ESRCH
    nil
  end
end

**ActiveJob in Rails 8.1 and Campfire: A Deep Dive**

Okay, this is intriguing! I need to fully understand how ActiveJob functions across different environments in this Rails 8.1 setup, especially in the context of Campfire. Let's break this down.

First, in **development**, `config/application.rb` confirms Rails 8.1 defaults. The key here is the default `config.active_job.queue_adapter`, which, *unless* explicitly overridden, is `:async`. This is significant! Because, looking at the `development.rb` environment file, the line setting the adapter to `resque` is commented out. So, when I run `bin/dev` or `bin/rails server` in development, ActiveJob *defaults* to `:async`. Meaning that background jobs are executed asynchronously using an in-process thread pool (`Concurrent::ThreadPoolExecutor`), completely bypassing the need for a separate Resque worker process. Brilliant.

Now, the **test** environment. This is where it gets interesting. I already knew that Rails uses `:test` for unit and integration tests, making `assert_enqueued_with` and `perform_enqueued_jobs` work as expected. But what about system tests, or automated browser tests managed by `ActionDispatch::SystemTestCase`? What adapter is *that* using? I'll need to verify that later, let's explore production before.

In **production**, the setup is clear. `production.rb` explicitly sets `config.active_job.queue_adapter = :resque`. And, looking at the `Dockerfile`, we see `CMD ["bin/boot"]`, which is pointing to `Procfile`. The `Procfile` then specifies the `web`, `redis`, and `workers: resque-pool` processes. This tells me that the queue adapter is Resque, so a dedicated Resque worker pool is managing jobs in production as intended.

The crucial question is, how does this affect our automated tests? Given that automated tests can run with `RAILS_ENV=development` (`bin/rails server`), `RAILS_ENV=production` (`bin/boot`), or the default `RAILS_ENV=test`, the behavior can vary.

So, I need to know: **what is `ActiveJob::Base.queue_adapter` actually set to in `development`, `test`, and `SystemTestCase` at runtime?** I'll use `bin/rails runner` to investigate the actual *current* configurations. That will tell me everything!

**Analyzing Webhook URL Validation for Bots**

Okay, so I'm thinking about how we handle webhook URLs, specifically in the context of our bots. It's clear that `.input` applies universally, regardless of whether the field type is `url` or `text`, and using something semantic like `form.url_field` is right, just like `form.email_field`. But, I need to make sure we're handling edge cases correctly.

First, what happens when someone *clears* a `<input type="url">` field, entering only whitespace? Browsers automatically strip that whitespace, so `"   "` becomes `""`, which is perfectly valid for an optional URL field. We need to mirror this on the server side; we should `.strip` the `webhook_url` and use `.presence` (`webhook_url.to_s.strip.presence`) so `"   "` effectively becomes `nil`, removing the webhook.

Now, what about invalid URLs? If someone tries to submit something like `javascript:alert(1)` or just plain text, how do we handle that? We definitely need URL validation. The question is, should `webhook_url` or `Webhook#url` validate that the input is a valid `URI::HTTP` with a non-blank `host`? Yes! But... what about `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or private network IPs?

Hold on. This is *critical*. **Should we allow `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, and private network URLs, or should we block them using something like `PrivateNetworkGuard`?**

Let's think about this from a testing perspective. How do our QA auto-tests actually work? They spin up a *local* HTTP server in the test runner, something like `http://127.0.0.1:4567/webhook` or `http://localhost:8080/webhook`. They then enter that into the web interface, trigger the bot, and assert that the local server gets the POST.

If we put a `PrivateNetworkGuard` on the bot webhooks, or validate the URL's "public-ness" with DNS, our QA tests would *break*. In a container without DNS, it would fail on *everything*, including `example.com` and `localhost`. And the tests themselves rely on loopback addresses to mock the server!   attr_reader :room, :message

  def initialize(room:, message:)
    @room, @message = room, message
  end

  def push
    build_payload.tap do |payload|
      push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
    end
  end

  private
    def build_payload
      if room.direct?
        build_direct_payload
      else
        build_shared_payload
      end
    end

    def build_direct_payload
      {
        title: message.creator.name,
        body: message.plain_text_body,
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def build_shared_payload
      {
        title: room.name,
        body: "#{message.creator.name}: #{message.plain_text_body}",
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(message.mentionees)
    end

      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_everything)

module ActionText
  class Fragment
    class << self
      def wrap(fragment_or_html)
        case fragment_or_html
        when self
          fragment_or_html
        when Nokogiri::XML::DocumentFragment # base class for all fragments
          new(fragment_or_html)
        else
          from_html(fragment_or_html)
        end
      end

      def from_html(html)
        new(ActionText::HtmlConversion.fragment_for_html(html.to_s.strip))
      end
    end

    attr_reader :source

    delegate :deconstruct, to: "source.elements"

    def initialize(source)
      @source = source
    end

    def find_all(selector)
      source.css(selector)
    end

    def update
      yield source = self.source.dup
      self.class.new(source)
    end

    def replace(selector)
      update do |source|
        source.css(selector).each do |node|
          replacement_node = yield(node)
          node.replace(replacement_node.to_s) if node != replacement_node
        end
      end
    end

    def to_plain_text
      @plain_text ||= PlainTextConversion.node_to_plain_text(source)
    end

    def to_html
      @html ||= HtmlConversion.node_to_html(source)
    end

    def to_s
      to_html
    end
  end

# :markup: markdown

module ActionText
  module PlainTextConversion
    extend self

    def node_to_plain_text(node)
      BottomUpReducer.new(node).reduce do |n, child_values|
        plain_text_for_node(n, child_values)
      end.then(&method(:remove_trailing_newlines))
    end

    private
      def plain_text_for_node(node, child_values)
        if respond_to?(plain_text_method_for_node(node), true)
          send(plain_text_method_for_node(node), node, child_values)
        else
          plain_text_for_child_values(child_values)
        end
      end

      def plain_text_method_for_node(node)
        :"plain_text_for_#{node.name}_node"
      end

      def plain_text_for_child_values(child_values)
        child_values.join
      end

      def plain_text_for_unsupported_node(node, _child_values)
        ""
      end

      %i[ script style].each do |element|
        alias_method :"plain_text_for_#{element}_node", :plain_text_for_unsupported_node
      end

      def plain_text_for_block(node, child_values)
        "#{remove_trailing_newlines(plain_text_for_child_values(child_values))}\n\n"
      end

      %i[ h1 p ].each do |element|
        alias_method :"plain_text_for_#{element}_node", :plain_text_for_block
      end

      def plain_text_for_list(node, child_values)
        "#{break_if_nested_list(node, plain_text_for_block(node, child_values))}"
      end

      %i[ ul ol ].each do |element|
        alias_method :"plain_text_for_#{element}_node", :plain_text_for_list
      end

      def plain_text_for_br_node(node, _child_values)
        "\n"
      end

      def plain_text_for_text_node(node, _child_values)
        remove_trailing_newlines(node.text)
      end

      def plain_text_for_div_node(node, child_values)
        "#{remove_trailing_newlines(plain_text_for_child_values(child_values))}\n"
      end

      def plain_text_for_figcaption_node(node, child_values)
        "[#{remove_trailing_newlines(plain_text_for_child_values(child_values))}]"
      end

      def plain_text_for_blockquote_node(node, child_values)
        text = plain_text_for_block(node, child_values)
        return "“”" if text.blank?

        text = text.dup
        text.insert(text.rindex(/\S/) + 1, "”")
        text.insert(text.index(/\S/), "“")
        text
      end

      def plain_text_for_li_node(node, child_values)
        bullet = bullet_for_li_node(node)
        text = remove_trailing_newlines(plain_text_for_child_values(child_values))
        indentation = indentation_for_li_node(node)

        "#{indentation}#{bullet} #{text}\n"
      end

      def remove_trailing_newlines(text)
        text.chomp("")
      end

      def bullet_for_li_node(node)
        if list_node_name_for_li_node(node) == "ol"
          index = node.parent.elements.index(node)
          "#{index + 1}."
        else
          "•"
        end
      end

      def list_node_name_for_li_node(node)
        node.ancestors.lazy.map(&:name).grep(/^[uo]l$/).first
      end

      def indentation_for_li_node(node)
        depth = list_node_depth_for_node(node)
        if depth > 1
          "  " * (depth - 1)
        end
      end

      def list_node_depth_for_node(node)
        node.ancestors.map(&:name).grep(/^[uo]l$/).count
      end

      def break_if_nested_list(node, text)
        if list_node_depth_for_node(node) > 0
          "\n#{text}"
        else
          text
        end
      end

      class BottomUpReducer # :nodoc:
        def initialize(node)
          @node = node
          @values = {}
        end

        def reduce(&block)
          traverse_bottom_up(@node) do |n|
            child_values = @values.values_at(*n.children)
            @values[n] = block.call(n, child_values)
          end
          @values[@node]
        end

        private
          def traverse_bottom_up(node, &block)
            call_stack, processing_stack = [ node ], []

            until call_stack.empty?
              node = call_stack.pop
              processing_stack.push(node)
              call_stack.concat node.children
            end

            processing_stack.reverse_each(&block)
          end
      end
  end
end

steps.reasoning_content:
**Decoding Responses and Orchestrating Background Jobs in Rails**

Okay, so I was looking at how we're handling character encodings in our HTTP responses. That `body encoding before: ASCII-8BIT` caught my eye. Even when we explicitly set `Content-Type` to `utf-8`, `Net::HTTP` was still returning the body as `ASCII-8BIT`. A quick fix of doing `.to_s.dup.force_encoding(Encoding::UTF_8).scrub` (or transcoding when there's a non-UTF-8 `charset` specified) seems to be the trick to prevent those pesky `Encoding::CompatibilityError` errors when a bot throws in some non-ASCII UTF-8 characters like those emojis.

Now, I was digging into `ApplicationSystemTestCase` and, more importantly, how it interacts with ActiveJob. The default `ActiveJob::Base.queue_adapter` is `ActiveJob::QueueAdapters::TestAdapter`. When a Capybara system test runs, `TestAdapter` shoves jobs into `enqueued_jobs` unless we explicitly call `perform_enqueued_jobs` or use `:async` or a `perform_enqueued_jobs` block. In `development` (like with `bin/dev` or `bin/rails server`), it's the `AsyncAdapter`, running jobs in background threads, and in `production` (through `bin/boot` or `Procfile`), we're using `ResqueAdapter` with `resque-pool`.

But, hold on a second! I had a moment of clarity regarding our automated QA tests! They could start our app in a few different ways, and each will affect our background jobs:

1.  `bin/dev` or `bin/rails server` (default `RAILS_ENV=development`) -> `AsyncAdapter` (background threads)
2.  `bin/boot` (`Procfile`, `RAILS_ENV=production`) -> `ResqueAdapter` + `redis-server` + `resque-pool`
3.  The tricky one: What if the QA harness uses something like `RAILS_ENV=production SECRET_KEY_BASE=... DISABLE_SSL=1 bin/rails server` without `resque-pool`? Or, what if they're running Playwright against `RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails server`?

Even if we start the server with `RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails server`, the `test.rb` setting overrules everything! If someone starts that with `RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails server` then ActiveJob uses `TestAdapter`. That's critical! `TestAdapter` puts jobs into an in-memory array and the job NEVER actually runs! And if the QA script starts with `RAILS_ENV=production` but *without* `resque-pool`, it pushes to Redis (or fails if Redis isn't running), but the job STILL doesn't run!

class WebPush::Pool
  attr_reader :delivery_pool, :invalidation_pool, :connection, :invalid_subscription_handler

  def initialize(invalid_subscription_handler:)
    @delivery_pool = Concurrent::ThreadPoolExecutor.new(max_threads: 50, queue_size: 10000)
    @invalidation_pool = Concurrent::FixedThreadPool.new(1)
    @connection = Net::HTTP::Persistent.new(name: "web_push", pool_size: 150)
    @invalid_subscription_handler = invalid_subscription_handler
  end

  def queue(payload, subscriptions)
    subscriptions.find_each do |subscription|
      deliver_later(payload, subscription)
    end
  end

  def shutdown
    connection.shutdown
    shutdown_pool(delivery_pool)
    shutdown_pool(invalidation_pool)
  end

  private
    def deliver_later(payload, subscription)
      # Ensure any AR operations happen before we post to the thread pool
      notification = subscription.notification(**payload)
      subscription_id = subscription.id

      delivery_pool.post do
        deliver(notification, subscription_id)
      rescue Exception => e
        Rails.logger.error "Error in WebPush::Pool.deliver: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
      end
    rescue Concurrent::RejectedExecutionError
    end

    def deliver(notification, id)
      notification.deliver(connection: connection)
    rescue WebPush::ExpiredSubscription, OpenSSL::OpenSSLError => ex
      invalidate_subscription_later(id) if invalid_subscription_handler
    end

    def invalidate_subscription_later(id)
      invalidation_pool.post do
        invalid_subscription_handler.call(id)
      rescue Exception => e
        Rails.logger.error "Error in WebPush::Pool.invalid_subscription_handler: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
      end
    end

    def shutdown_pool(pool)
      pool.shutdown
      pool.kill unless pool.wait_for_termination(1)

class Room < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all do

    end

    def revoke_from(users)
      destroy_by user: users
    end

  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy

Bots are represented in the `users` table with `role: :bot` (`enum :role, %i[ member administrator bot ]`):

- **`creator_id`**: Foreign key to `users` (`belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", optional: true`), recording which chat member created the bot. Because `User::Role#can_administer?` checks `administrator? || self == record&.creator`, creators and administrators automatically have permission to manage a bot while other regular members do not.
- **`bot_token` & `bot_key`**: Active bots receive a unique 24-character `SecureRandom.base58` `bot_token` on creation. The externally visible bot code (`User#bot_key`) is `"#{id}-#{bot_token}"`. `User.authenticate_bot(bot_key)` looks up the active bot by primary key `id` and compares `bot_token` in constant time via `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare`.
- **Deactivation (Deletion)**: Deleting a bot calls `User#deactivate`, which sets `status: :deactivated`, clears `bot_token: nil`, and removes non-direct room memberships while preserving historical messages authored by the bot.
- **Room Memberships**: Because bots are `User` records with `status: :active`, they automatically join all open rooms via `after_create_commit :grant_membership_to_open_rooms` (and `Rooms::Open#grant_access_to_all_users`) and appear alongside human users in closed/direct room member selectors (`User.active`). Human-only flows (`/account/edit` member list, `/session`, session transfers, IP bans) scope queries with `User.without_bots`.

## Bot HTTP API (`Messages::ByBotsController`)

- **Endpoint**: `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` (`constraints: { room_id: /[^\/]+/, bot_key: /[^\/]+/ }`).
- **Raw Body Handling**: `curl -d "..."` sends `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` by default even though the payload is raw text (which may contain `%`, `+`, `&`, etc.). `Messages::ByBotsController` sets `wrap_parameters false` and `request.request_parameters = {}` in `process_action` before Rails instrumentation accesses `request.filtered_parameters`, preventing Rack/Rails form/JSON parameter parsers from raising `400 Bad Request` on raw bodies. The raw UTF-8 body is read from `request.raw_post`.
- **Validation & Extension Point for Attachments**: `Message` validates `ensure_body_or_attachment_present` (`body.blank? && body.body&.attachables.blank? && !attachment?`). If future features add file attachment uploads for bots (e.g., binary bodies by `Content-Type` or `multipart/form-data`), `Messages::ByBotsController#create` can attach the file and call `@message.process_attachment` before `@message.broadcast_create`.
- **Broadcasts & Push Notifications**: Setting `Current.user = bot` sets `message.creator = bot`. Saving triggers `Room#receive` (`unread_memberships` + `Room::PushMessageJob`), and `@message.broadcast_create` appends the message via Turbo Streams and notifies `UnreadRoomsChannel`.
"
}

steps.message:
I have implemented bot mention webhooks and synchronous/asynchronous bot replies in Campfire:

- **Webhook Model & Bot Form (`Webhook`, `User::Bot`, `BotsController`, `app/views/bots/_form.html.erb`)**:
  - Added the `webhooks` table (`CreateWebhooks` migration) and `Webhook` model (`has_one :webhook, dependent: :destroy, autosave: true` on `User` via `User::Bot`), exposing `webhook_url` and `webhook_url=` with HTTP/HTTPS URL validation.
  - Added the optional `"Webhook URL"` field (both `<label>` text and `placeholder`) to `/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit`. Saving with an empty webhook URL removes the bot's webhook, and deactivating a bot also destroys its webhook.
- **@-Mention Autocomplete & Asynchronous Webhook Dispatch (`Room#receive`, `Message::Mentionee`, `Webhook::DeliveryJob`)**:
  - Active bots in a room appear in `/autocompletable/users` alongside human members and use ActionText mention attachables.
  - When a user creates a message mentioning an active bot with a webhook, `Room#receive` enqueues `Webhook::DeliveryJob` in the background so webhook calls never slow down posting a message (and bot-authored messages do not trigger bot webhooks).
- **Mention Payload & Bot Replies (`Webhook#deliver`)**:
  - Sends `POST` with `Content-Type: application/json` containing `event` (`"mention"`), `author` (`{ id, name }`), `room` (`{ id, name, reply_to }`), and `message` (`{ id, body: { text, html }, link }`), where `message.body.text` strips only that bot's own `@`-mention and paths (`room.reply_to` and `message.link`) are relative.
  - Replies with `200` and `Content-Type: text/plain` or `text/html` post and broadcast the response body into the room as the bot's message; `204` posts nothing so the bot may reply asynchronously via `room.reply_to`.

I will now submit the final output.
